lessonTitle: Test Planning: Procedures, Verification Methods and Instruments

blocks.text: A team tests a prototype clamp by hanging weights until 'it looks fine', using a bathroom scale for the load and a ruler for the deflection. The requirement is a deflection within plus or minus 0.05 mm at 12 kN. The ruler resolves 1 mm, so the test could never have shown the requirement was met or failed. A test plan decides, before any hardware is loaded, what will be measured, with what, and what result means pass.

blocks.markdown: A **test plan** links the requirements to evidence. It answers four questions for every requirement: *how* will it be verified (test, analysis, inspection), *by what procedure*, *with what instruments*, and *what result counts as a pass*. Writing the plan during design exposes requirements that cannot be verified and stops the team from discovering, at the end, that the only suitable instrument was never ordered.

blocks.title: Test procedure
blocks.text: A test procedure is a written, step-by-step instruction that another competent person can follow to obtain the same result. It contains: purpose and the requirement(s) addressed; **setup** (specimen, fixtures, instruments with identifiers, environment); the **sequence of steps**; the **measurements** to be recorded, with units and sampling; the **pass criteria**, stated in numbers; **safety checks** (hazards, guards, limits, abort conditions, personal protective equipment); and the record form to be completed.

rows: Performance must be observed on real hardware
Proof-load test, measured deflection and permanent set
Hardware does not yet exist or test is impractical
Finite element or hand calculation report
A feature can be examined or measured without operating
Rated load marked in letters at least 10 mm high
Guard closes and interlock stops machine
blocks.caption: Mapping requirements to verification methods.

blocks.markdown: **Mapping requirements to methods.** Build a table with one row per requirement: ID, requirement text, verification method, procedure reference, instrument, pass criterion and status. Every requirement must appear at least once, and every test should serve at least one requirement; a test without a requirement wastes effort and a requirement without a test is unverified. Where several methods are used (analysis at design stage, test on the prototype) both appear.

**Choosing instruments.** The instrument must be good enough to resolve the tolerance being verified. A common rule of thumb is that the instrument's total uncertainty should be no more than one quarter of the tolerance, that is a **test accuracy ratio** (TAR) of at least 4:1. In addition the **range** should be matched to the expected value: readings in the middle part of the range (roughly 20% to 80% of full scale) are the most accurate, because accuracy is often quoted as a percentage of *full scale*, so a small reading on a large range has a large relative uncertainty, and a reading beyond the range damages or saturates the instrument.

blocks.caption: t is the half-width of the tolerance (the plus-or-minus value) and u_inst the instrument's uncertainty in the same unit. TAR of 4 or more is a typical rule of thumb, not a law.

blocks.title: Instrument for a dimensional tolerance
blocks.prompt: A critical dimension has a tolerance of $\pm0.05$ mm. A vernier caliper has an uncertainty of $\pm0.03$ mm and a micrometer $\pm0.005$ mm. Which is suitable under a 4:1 rule?
blocks.answer: The micrometer is suitable; the caliper cannot resolve the tolerance.

blocks.title: Choosing a load cell range
blocks.prompt: A proof test applies about 12 kN and must verify a load within $\pm120$ N. Load cell A has a 20 kN range and an accuracy of $\pm0.1\%$ of full scale; load cell B has a 100 kN range with the same percentage accuracy. Which should be used?

steps.text: Cell A: $0.001\times20\,000=20$ N and the reading uses $12/20=60\%$ of range, so $\mathrm{TAR}=120/20=6$.
Cell B: $0.001\times100\,000=100$ N, $\mathrm{TAR}=1.2$, and the reading is only 12% of range.

blocks.answer: Use load cell A: 20 N uncertainty (TAR 6) and 60% of range; cell B fails the 4:1 rule.

items: State the requirement and the pass criterion in numbers.
List the setup, with instrument IDs and calibration status.
Write numbered steps including loading rate, hold time and number of repeats.
Specify what is recorded and in what units.
Add safety checks and an abort condition before loading begins.

blocks.title: Decide pass criteria before testing
blocks.text: A pass criterion written after seeing the data will unconsciously follow the data. Write it, with its uncertainty allowance, in the plan.

blocks.title: Range is not the same as accuracy
blocks.text: A large-range instrument may read small values with poor relative accuracy, and a small-range instrument may be destroyed by overload. Check both the range for the expected value and the margin to overload.

points: A test procedure contains setup, measurements, numerical pass criteria and safety checks so that anyone can repeat it.
Every requirement is mapped to test, analysis, inspection or demonstration, with a procedure and instrument.
Choose instruments so that TAR $\ge4$ and the expected value falls in the useful part of the range.

questions.stem: A written test procedure lists the specimen, instruments, loading steps and the readings to record, but gives no pass or fail limits. What is missing?

options.text: Numerical pass criteria stated in advance

questions.correctOptionText: Numerical pass criteria stated in advance

distractorRationale.a: Correct: without limits the outcome cannot be judged objectively.
distractorRationale.c: Results do not exist until the test is run.
distractorRationale.d: Suppliers are not part of a test procedure.

questions.explanation: A procedure needs pass criteria in numbers so that the result is decided by the data. Otherwise the interpretation can drift toward what the team hopes to see.

questions.stem: Before a hydraulic proof test of a prototype cylinder, which safety check belongs in the procedure?

options.text: Confirm that a relief valve is set below the test limit, guards are in place, and an abort condition is defined
Increase pressure quickly to save time
Remove the guard to watch the test closely
Skip the check if the cylinder has been tested before

questions.correctOptionText: Confirm that a relief valve is set below the test limit, guards are in place, and an abort condition is defined

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it limits the consequence of a failure and defines when to stop.
distractorRationale.c: Removing a guard exposes people to the hazard.
distractorRationale.d: Each test needs its own safety check.

questions.explanation: Safety checks are part of the procedure. They keep the test within the safe limits of the rig and allow it to be stopped if something unexpected happens.

questions.stem: Which verification method suits the requirement 'the nameplate shall show the rated load in characters at least 10 mm high'?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the feature can be checked by examining or measuring it.

questions.explanation: Inspection verifies features by looking at or measuring them. A printed character height does not need operation of the product.

questions.stem: In a verification matrix one requirement has no method listed, and one planned test does not link to any requirement. What should be done?

options.text: Add a method for the requirement and either link or remove the unlinked test

questions.correctOptionText: Add a method for the requirement and either link or remove the unlinked test

distractorRationale.a: Correct: each requirement needs verification and each test must serve a purpose.
distractorRationale.b: The requirement would stay unverified and the test would waste effort.
distractorRationale.d: Repeating a pointless test does not help.

questions.explanation: Two-way mapping avoids unverified requirements and redundant tests. Every requirement is assigned a method and every test traced back to a requirement.

questions.stem: A tolerance of $\pm0.5$ N m must be verified with a torque wrench of total uncertainty $\pm0.4$ N m. Under a 4:1 rule, what is the conclusion?

options.text: The wrench is not suitable, since TAR is only 1.25
The wrench is suitable because its uncertainty is below the tolerance
The wrench is suitable because torque wrenches are always accurate

questions.correctOptionText: The wrench is not suitable, since TAR is only 1.25

distractorRationale.b: Being just below the tolerance is not enough for a 4:1 rule.
distractorRationale.c: Accuracy depends on the instrument and calibration.

questions.explanation: The test accuracy ratio compares the tolerance half-width with the instrument uncertainty. A ratio of 1.25 means the instrument's own uncertainty consumes most of the tolerance.

questions.stem: A dimension has a tolerance of $\pm0.08$ mm and a measuring instrument has an uncertainty of $\pm0.02$ mm. Compute the test accuracy ratio (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: The ratio is $0.08/0.02=4$, which just meets the 4:1 rule of thumb. Any larger instrument uncertainty would fail it.

questions.stem: A torque requirement has a tolerance of $\pm0.6$ N m. Using a 4:1 test accuracy ratio, what is the largest instrument uncertainty, in N m, that is acceptable?
questions.explanation: The maximum uncertainty is $0.6/4=0.15$ N m. An instrument with a larger uncertainty cannot resolve the tolerance reliably.

questions.stem: A pressure must be verified to $\pm0.4$ MPa. A gauge has an accuracy of $\pm0.5\%$ of full scale. For a 4:1 test accuracy ratio, what is the largest full-scale range, in MPa, that can be used?
questions.explanation: The allowed uncertainty is $0.4/4=0.1$ MPa and $0.005\times FS=0.1$ gives $FS=20$ MPa. A larger range would have too large an uncertainty.

questions.stem: Write a test procedure for verifying that a hand-operated jack lifts a 500 kg load through 0.2 m with no permanent deformation. Include the setup, the measurements, a numerical pass criterion and the safety checks.
markingGuide: Setup: jack, test mass or load cell, rigid stable base, dial gauge or ruler for lift height, instrument IDs and calibration status
Steps in order: inspect, place load, lift 0.2 m, hold, lower, repeat for stated number of trials
Measurements: load, lift height, permanent deformation, with units and resolution
Pass criterion in numbers (for example lifted 0.2 m, permanent set below a stated limit)
Safety checks: stable support, load restraint, personnel clear, abort condition
questions.explanation: A good procedure can be followed by someone else. It has defined limits and safety measures established before anything is loaded.

questions.stem: A requirements list contains: (R1) the frame deflects no more than 1.5 mm at 8 kN, (R2) the mass is at most 14 kg, (R3) the frame has a natural frequency above 40 Hz and (R4) the rated load is labelled. Produce a verification matrix choosing methods and say how you would select the instrument for R1 so that the tolerance can be resolved.
markingGuide: R1 test (deflection under load); R2 inspection by weighing; R3 analysis at the design stage with test later; R4 inspection
Pass criteria with numbers for each requirement
Instrument for R1: load cell with expected 8 kN placed in middle of range, uncertainty small relative to tolerance
Test accuracy ratio of 4:1 or better for deflection gauge relative to the tolerance
Each requirement mapped and each test traced
questions.explanation: Each requirement is assigned a suitable method and a numerical pass criterion. For R1 the instrument must resolve the deflection tolerance with a margin and have a range that matches the expected load.
